question: When a chatbot answers your question, the trained model is doing what?
correctAnswer: Inference: using the trained model to generate a response
incorrectAnswers: Training: updating its weights from your message
Pretraining: reading a new batch of web text
Labeling: tagging your message for a dataset
explanation: Inference is the process of running an already trained model on an input prompt to produce a response. Training happens earlier and is what sets the model's weights.

question: In the analogy of a model going to school, what matches a graduate applying their knowledge on the job?
correctAnswer: Inference
incorrectAnswers: Training
Data labeling
Tokenization
explanation: Training is the schooling phase where the model learns from data. Inference is the deployed model applying what it learned to new inputs, and it cannot happen without training first.

question: Which of these can a single token be for a language model?
correctAnswer: A whole word, part of a word, a character or a byte
incorrectAnswers: Always exactly one whole word
Always exactly one full sentence
Always a fixed block of eight letters
explanation: Tokens are the smallest units a language model works with. Depending on the tokenizer, a token can be a word, a subword, a single character or even a byte.

question: Why must text be split into tokens before a model can use it?
correctAnswer: Models only process numbers, so text is mapped to numeric IDs
incorrectAnswers: Tokens encrypt the text so it stays private
Splitting removes spelling and grammar errors
Tokens shrink the text so it downloads faster
explanation: A neural network works on numbers, not letters. A tokenizer breaks text into pieces and turns each piece into a number the model can process.

question: Many tokenizers keep common words whole but split rare words into smaller pieces. What does this gain?
correctAnswer: Good coverage with a small vocabulary and almost no unknown tokens
incorrectAnswers: Every word gets its own unique token ID
Text always becomes one token per character
The model no longer needs any vocabulary at all
explanation: Subword tokenizers sit between word-level and character-level splitting. Rare words can be built from known pieces, so the vocabulary stays small and unknown tokens are rare.

question: What is a main downside of splitting text into single characters instead of words?
correctAnswer: The model has to process much longer sequences
incorrectAnswers: The vocabulary grows to hundreds of thousands of entries
Many words turn into unknown tokens
Rare words can no longer be represented
explanation: Every word can be built from characters, so the vocabulary is small and unknown tokens are rare. The trade-off is that each text turns into far more tokens.

question: What is a language model's context window?
correctAnswer: The text it can reference while generating, like a working memory
incorrectAnswers: The full set of data it was trained on
The date range its knowledge covers
The number of users it can serve at once
explanation: The context window is the amount of text the model can look at while it writes a response. It is separate from the much larger body of data used to train the model.

question: In a chat request, which of these count toward the context window?
correctAnswer: The system prompt, the conversation so far, and the model's reply
incorrectAnswers: Only the user's newest message
Only the system prompt
Only the reply the model generates
explanation: Everything in the request uses context space: the system prompt, all previous messages and the new message. The output the model generates for that turn counts too.

question: What tends to happen as you pack more and more tokens into a model's context?
correctAnswer: Accuracy and recall start to degrade
incorrectAnswers: Accuracy keeps improving without limit
The model retrains itself on the new text
Responses become fully deterministic
explanation: More context is not automatically better. As the token count grows, the model's accuracy and recall degrade, an effect known as context rot, so what you put in context matters.

question: What does the temperature setting control in a generative model?
correctAnswer: How random the model's output is
incorrectAnswers: The maximum length of the response
How quickly tokens are produced
How many documents are retrieved
explanation: Temperature is a setting that controls the degree of randomness in the model's output. Higher values give more varied text and lower values give more predictable text.

question: For which task is a low temperature usually the better choice?
correctAnswer: Writing precise technical documentation
incorrectAnswers: Brainstorming names for a new product
Writing a fantasy short story
Generating many different slogan ideas
explanation: Low temperature makes the most likely tokens even more likely, so output is more predictable. That suits tasks that need precision, while high temperature suits creative work.

question: If you send the same prompt twice with temperature set to 0, will you always get identical output?
correctAnswer: Not necessarily; outputs can still differ between calls
incorrectAnswers: Yes, temperature 0 guarantees identical output
Only if the prompt is shorter than 100 tokens
Only if both calls come from the same user
explanation: Temperature 0 makes the model stick to the most likely answers, but API results are still not fully deterministic. Identical inputs can produce different outputs across calls.

question: What does it mean when an AI model hallucinates?
correctAnswer: It gives plausible-sounding output that is factually wrong
incorrectAnswers: It refuses to answer a harmless question
It stops responding partway through
It repeats its training data word for word
explanation: A hallucination is output that sounds believable but is false, irrelevant or made up. The confident tone is what makes it easy to miss.

question: Why can a language model state something false in a confident tone?
correctAnswer: It is built to produce plausible text, not to check facts
incorrectAnswers: It deliberately lies to save computing power
It reads from a corrupted database at runtime
Its temperature is set too low
explanation: Language models are optimized to produce text that sounds right. Nothing in that goal guarantees accuracy, and gaps or errors in training data can also become wrong answers.

question: Which approach helps reduce hallucinations?
correctAnswer: Grounding answers in a curated knowledge base with citations
incorrectAnswers: Raising the temperature as high as possible
Removing all instructions from the prompt
Asking the model for much longer answers
explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation limits answers to trusted material, often with citations. Clear prompt rules, such as telling the model to say when it does not know, also help.

question: What does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) add before a model answers?
correctAnswer: It pulls relevant outside documents into the prompt
incorrectAnswers: It retrains the model on the user's question
It doubles the model's number of parameters
It translates the question into another language
explanation: RAG finds relevant material from a knowledge base outside the model's training data and adds it to the prompt. The model then answers using both the question and that material.

question: A company wants its chatbot to know this week's policy changes. Why is RAG often picked over retraining?
correctAnswer: It adds new information without the cost of retraining
incorrectAnswers: It permanently rewrites the model's weights
It works without storing the new documents anywhere
It makes the model's context window unlimited
explanation: With RAG, new documents are stored and retrieved at question time. That is a cheaper way to give a model fresh information than retraining it.

question: How does fine-tuning differ from simply writing a better prompt?
correctAnswer: Fine-tuning trains the model further and updates its parameters
incorrectAnswers: Fine-tuning only changes the wording of the prompt
Fine-tuning swaps the model's tokenizer for a new one
Fine-tuning attaches a search engine at answer time
explanation: Fine-tuning is a second, task-specific training pass on a pretrained model that refines its parameters. A prompt only changes the input; the model itself stays the same.

question: What is catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuning?
correctAnswer: Fine-tuning causes the model to lose some core knowledge
incorrectAnswers: The model deletes the fine-tuning data after training
The model forgets earlier messages in a chat
The model refuses to answer questions on old topics
explanation: Training a model hard on a narrow new dataset can destabilize what it learned before. Using parameter-efficient methods or a smaller learning rate makes this less likely.

question: What is an embedding in machine learning?
correctAnswer: A list of numbers that represents an item and its meaning
incorrectAnswers: A short text summary of a document
A password that unlocks a model's weights
A picture inserted inside a prompt
explanation: Embeddings turn things like words or images into numeric vectors. Related items end up with similar vectors, which lets software compare meaning and find similar content.

question: How does a diffusion model generate a new image?
correctAnswer: It starts from random noise and removes it step by step
incorrectAnswers: It stitches together pieces of stored photos
It writes the image one pixel row at a time from a caption
It sharpens a blurry copy of an existing image
explanation: During training, the model learns to reverse a process that slowly adds noise to images. To generate, it begins with pure noise and denoises it until a new image appears.

question: How do generative models differ from traditional classification models?
correctAnswer: They create new content instead of only assigning labels
incorrectAnswers: They only sort existing data into categories
They can only work with numbers, never text
They need no training data at all
explanation: A classifier predicts a label from features, such as spam or not spam. A generative model works the other way, producing new content like text or images.

question: What does a model's reliable knowledge cutoff tell you?
correctAnswer: The date through which its knowledge is most complete and reliable
incorrectAnswers: The date the model will be retired
The last date it was updated with a security patch
The date its context window was last increased
explanation: A model learns from data collected up to a point in time. Its reliable knowledge cutoff marks the date through which that knowledge is most extensive, so later events may be missing.

question: What is the difference between a model's parameters and its hyperparameters?
correctAnswer: Parameters are learned in training; hyperparameters are set by people
incorrectAnswers: Parameters are set by people; hyperparameters are learned
Both are learned automatically during inference
Parameters only exist in image models
explanation: Parameters are the weights and biases a model learns during training. Hyperparameters, such as how long to train, are settings people adjust between training runs.

question: Right after pretraining, why is a language model not yet a good assistant?
correctAnswer: It learned to predict the next word, not to follow instructions
incorrectAnswers: It has not yet been given any parameters
It cannot read text until it is fine-tuned
Its context window is still set to zero
explanation: Pretraining teaches a model to predict the next word from a huge amount of text. Extra steps such as fine-tuning and RLHF are used to make it follow instructions and answer helpfully.
